title: IBM Suffers Worst Day in 115-Year History as Stock Crashes 25 Percent, Erasing Nearly $70 Billion in Value
excerpt: CEO Arvind Krishna's rare profit warning exposed how the AI revolution is disrupting even the companies trying to sell it, and Wall Street is now debating whether Big Blue should be broken apart.
body:
IBM suffered the worst single-day stock decline in its 115-year history this week, plunging 25% and erasing nearly $70 billion in market capitalization after CEO Arvind Krishna — one of the most prominent Indian-origin executives in corporate America — issued a rare profit warning that caught Wall Street completely off guard.

## What Happened

The crisis began when IBM's board of directors, after what the Wall Street Journal described as an intense internal debate, decided to pre-announce disappointing second-quarter results rather than wait for the scheduled earnings release a week later.

"This quarter we faltered," Krishna wrote in an investor letter published hours before markets opened on Tuesday. The board had debated whether to take the unusual step of issuing the warning early, ultimately deciding that transparency would build credibility with investors — even if the short-term price would be severe.

IBM shares cratered 25% to $216.44, the worst day in the century-old company's history. The stock had been trading near all-time highs, buoyed by its positioning as an AI infrastructure winner.

## The AI Disruption Behind the Numbers

The results revealed an uncomfortable truth: the artificial intelligence revolution is disrupting IBM even as the company tries to help its customers navigate the same transformation.

Krishna attributed the miss to poor execution, saying the company "did not adapt and move quickly enough" as customers suddenly shifted their budgets toward servers, storage, and memory products in anticipation of tariff-driven price increases. Infrastructure revenue fell 7% — faster and harder than expected — with the company's storied mainframe division hit particularly hard.

According to Barron's, even IBM's legacy mainframes — massive computers that banks and credit-card networks rely on to process billions of transactions — couldn't escape the downturn.

## Wall Street Reacts

The fallout has been swift. Oppenheimer downgraded IBM stock from "Outperform" to a neutral "Perform" rating, while HSBC had already slashed its rating to the equivalent of "Sell" with a $191 price target. BofA Securities maintained a buy rating but cut its price target from $330 to $280.

More dramatically, discussions have begun on Wall Street about whether IBM should be broken apart, or whether an activist investor might target the company. HSBC recommended investors construct a "synthetic IBM" portfolio by buying shares of IonQ, SAP, Accenture, and HP Inc. instead.

## The Arvind Krishna Factor

Don Bilson, head of event-driven research at Gordon Haskett, issued a pointed warning: "He needs to get this straightened out quickly because the last thing any 63-year-old CEO can afford is being stigmatized as a spotty executor that is responsible for historic selloffs."

Krishna, who was born in Andhra Pradesh and holds degrees from IIT Kanpur and the University of Illinois, has led IBM since April 2020. His tenure has focused on pivoting the company toward hybrid cloud and AI, including the $34 billion acquisition of Red Hat. For the Indian diaspora in tech — which has watched Indian-origin leaders rise to the top of Microsoft, Google, and Adobe — IBM's struggles are a reminder that even the most accomplished executives face forces beyond their control.

IBM will report full quarterly results next week.

*Sources: Wall Street Journal, Barron's, Investor's Business Daily*
author: Diaspora Desk
